title: Chukat: Aaron dies (Numbers 20:22–29)
hook: all the house of Israel weeps thirty days for the man who pursued peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses struck the rock he was told to speak to, and the commentators still argue about why it mattered. Your line was speak to the rock.

At some funerals the room is full of people who don't seem to fit together. Old rivals side by side. A cousin who hasn't spoken to the family in years. Ask why, and the answer is usually the same: he was the one who made peace. He'd call both sides. The Torah describes a mourning like that. Not long after Miriam's death, the people reach a mountain called Hor, and Aaron, the first high priest, climbs it for the last time.
screen: `OLD RIVALS SIDE BY SIDE.` → `THE ONE WHO MADE PEACE.` → `AARON CLIMBS MOUNT HOR.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase: God tells Moses to take Aaron and his son Eleazar up Mount Hor, in sight of the whole community. On the mountain, Moses takes off Aaron's priestly garments, the ones made back in Exodus, and puts them on Eleazar. Aaron dies there, on the top of the mountain. Moses and Eleazar come down. No speech, no last words. Then the people see that Aaron is gone, and the Torah says they wept for Aaron thirty days, "even all the house of Israel." All the house. Rashi says it means everyone, men and women alike, because Aaron pursued peace, making peace between people who had quarreled and between husbands and wives. A collection called Avot de-Rabbi Natan tells how. When two people had fallen out, Aaron would sit with the first and say: your friend is beating his chest, saying, how can I face him, I wronged him. Then he'd go to the second and say the same thing. When the two met, they embraced. A gentle story, and a slightly mischievous one: Aaron helped each believe the other wanted to make up, until they did. Hillel, in the Mishnah, made Aaron the model for everyone: be among the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. Pursuing. Peace here isn't something you wait for. You run after it. And when the man who ran after it died, the tradition says, everyone came.
screen: `THE GARMENTS PASS TO ELEAZAR.` · `ALL THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL WEPT.` · `HE WENT TO EACH SIDE.` · `LOVING PEACE, PURSUING PEACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who brought people back together: the one who made the first phone call, who sat with both sides, who wouldn't let a family drift apart. They might be living, or they might be gone. Picture their face and the way they did it, and if it's someone you've lost, let yourself miss them for a few breaths.
Chukat. The portion where Aaron dies on Mount Hor, and all the house of Israel weeps thirty days for the man who pursued peace.
Your line: all the house wept. Aaron's students love peace, and run after it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Aaron's death is read in the portion of Chukat, and Hillel's saying about being a student of Aaron, loving and pursuing peace, is among the best-known lines of Pirkei Avot, often taught to children.

He was high priest, and the law told the whole people how long to mourn.
